title: Conjecture 2 (Conjecture 6.1 [1])
statement_text: For any graph $G$, the collection $\{\mathcal{C}_{k}(G)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ uniquely determines $G$.
context_text: Asgarli, Krehbiel, Levinson and Russell conjectured that the collection of all $k$-colouring graphs of $G$, or equivalently the collection of all generalised chromatic polynomials $\{\pi^{(H)}_{G}(k)\}_{H\in\mathcal{G}}$, forms a complete graph invariant. This is the weaker of their two conjectures on the topic.
paper_contribution: Confirmed by proving Theorem 4: for any graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and any $k > 5n^2$, the single colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ already uniquely determines $G$ up to isomorphism.

title: Conjecture 3 (Conjecture 6.2 [1])
statement_text: There exists some function $f:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that for any graph $G$, the collection $\{\mathcal{C}_{k}(G)\}^{f(G)}_{k=1}$ uniquely determines $G$.
context_text: This is the stronger companion conjecture to Conjecture 6.1 of Asgarli et al., asserting that finitely many colouring graphs (depending on $G$) suffice to reconstruct $G$, rather than the full infinite collection.
paper_contribution: Confirmed as a consequence of Theorem 4: taking $f(G) = 5n^2 + 1$ where $n = |V(G)|$, a single colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ with $k > 5n^2$ suffices to uniquely determine $G$.

title: Problem 11
statement_text: For which graphs $H$ does there exist an $H^{\prime}$ such that $\pi_{G}^{(H^{\prime})}$ determines $\pi_{G}^{(H)}$ for every graph $G$?
context_text: All colourings are proper, and a $k$-colouring uses colours from $\{1,\dots,k\}$. The $k$-colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ has the $k$-colourings of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they differ at exactly one vertex of $G$. For graphs $G,H$, the generalised chromatic polynomial $\pi_G^{(H)}(k)$ (introduced by Asgarli, Krehbiel, Levinson and Russell) is the number of vertex subsets of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ inducing a subgraph isomorphic to $H$, as a function of $k$; the authors prove it is always a polynomial in $k$. Thus $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$ is the chromatic polynomial and $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ counts edges of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$. Here $\pi_G^{(H')}$ determines $\pi_G^{(H)}$ if any two graphs $G_1,G_2$ with $\pi_{G_1}^{(H')}=\pi_{G_2}^{(H')}$ satisfy $\pi_{G_1}^{(H)}=\pi_{G_2}^{(H)}$ (the interesting case being $H'\ne H$; the paper does not say so explicitly). Asgarli et al. conjectured that $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ determines $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$, which remains unverified. The authors show that for connected $H$ there is a finite family $\mathcal{F}(H)$ of graphs, not containing $H$ and not depending on $G$, such that $\{\pi_G^{(F)}:F\in\mathcal{F}(H)\}$ determines $\pi_G^{(H)}$, which motivates asking when a single graph suffices. Since $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ is an induced subgraph of the Cartesian product of $|V(G)|$ copies of $K_k$, the problem is only interesting when $H$ is an induced subgraph of such a product.

title: Problem 12
statement_text: Is there a finite set of graphs $H_{1},\dotsc,H_{t}$ such that, for almost every $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,\frac{1}{2})$, if $\pi_{G^{\prime}}^{(H_{i})}=\pi_{G}^{(H_{i})}$ for all $i$ then $G^{\prime}\cong G$?
context_text: All colourings are proper, and a $k$-colouring uses colours from $\{1,\dots,k\}$. The $k$-colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ has the $k$-colourings of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they differ at exactly one vertex of $G$. For graphs $G,H$, the generalised chromatic polynomial $\pi_G^{(H)}(k)$ (introduced by Asgarli, Krehbiel, Levinson and Russell) is the number of vertex subsets of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ inducing a subgraph isomorphic to $H$, as a function of $k$; the authors prove it is always a polynomial in $k$. Thus $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$ is the chromatic polynomial and $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ counts edges of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$. $\mathcal{G}(n,\frac12)$ is the random graph on $n$ vertices with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$. The authors prove that for every $n$-vertex graph $G$ and every $k>5n^2$, $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ determines $G$ up to isomorphism (confirming two conjectures of Asgarli et al.), but that no finite family of generalised chromatic polynomials is a complete graph invariant. Bollobás, Pebody and Riordan conjectured that almost every graph is determined by its chromatic polynomial; this problem is a weakening of that conjecture, asking whether finitely many generalised chromatic polynomials suffice for typical graphs.
